entry.title: I Studied the Impact of Parents’ 9/11 Trauma on Their Children. Then I Understood My Father’s Silence.

link.title: I Studied the Impact of Parents’ 9/11 Trauma on Their Children. Then I Understood My Father’s Silence.

entry.content: When I was 5, we’d often visit my grandparents on the weekends. Their small apartment filled quickly with my father’s siblings—my aunts and uncles—and their children, my cousins. The adults would engage in animated conversation, usually about current events, while we, the dozen or so kids, kept ourselves busy inventing games. Our favorite games unfolded beneath the dining table; at times, we transformed it into a bus, traveling to unfamiliar places, as we took turns playing different roles: the driver, the passenger, and the ticket officer.

entry.title: Newsweek interview: 9/11 Responders’ Trauma May Have Affected Their Children, Study Finds

link.title: Newsweek interview: 9/11 Responders’ Trauma May Have Affected Their Children, Study Finds

entry.content:
Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, a study has found the children of World Trade Center responders may have been impacted by their parents’ trauma, even though they did not see the destruction themselves.

The study, conducted by researchers at Columbia University, found the children of 9/11 responders who developed post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after the terrorist attacks were more likely to have psychological conditions, such as anxiety and depression.

entry.title: 9/11 Responders Passed Effects of Trauma to Their Children

link.title: 9/11 Responders Passed Effects of Trauma to Their Children

entry.content: Although it’s been 25 years since the World Trade Center collapsed after terrorists flew commercial airplanes into each of the center’s two towers, the trauma experienced by many first responders and recovery workers is still being felt by their children.

entry.title: When Everything Becomes ‘Trauma,’ What Happens to Resilience?

link.title: When Everything Becomes ‘Trauma,’ What Happens to Resilience?

entry.content: The noise of the rotor was deafening as I held my daughter tightly on my lap, terrified that she might slip from my arms and be pulled out through the still-open door of the rescue helicopter. Below us, the Swiss Alps were breathtaking, lush green valleys carved between rugged mountains, water rushing in thin white streams. It was the tenth day of what had been meant to be a relaxed two-week summer vacation, abruptly interrupted by a major flood. Who would have imagined that such a deadly flood would occur high in the mountains? Only when we arrived at the hotel in Zurich did we learn of the larger catastrophe unfolding in the United States, Hurricane Katrina. Watching the images on television, I remember thinking that if I had to experience a flood, I was fortunate to have lived through one in Switzerland. Yet that moment also deepened my growing interest in psychological trauma and how memory shapes our resilience or vulnerability to its lingering effects.
